t: Equalize Strings by Adding or Removing Characters at Ends — Longest Common Substring
o: Operations only touch the ends of `initial`, so the characters of `initial` that survive must form a contiguous substring s, and everything deleted from the front/back plus everything appended must turn it into `target`. That means s must also appear as a contiguous substring of `target`: the cost is (|initial| − |s|) removals + (|target| − |s|) additions = n + m − 2|s|. Maximizing |s| — the longest common substring — minimizes operations. Example 1: common substring "cde" gives 5 + 4 − 6 = 3; example 2: only length-1 overlaps exist, giving 4 + 4 − 2 = 6.
k: Surviving characters of initial form one contiguous block, which must occur contiguously in target.
Answer = len(initial) + len(target) − 2 · (longest common substring length).
Classic LCSubstring DP: dp[i][j] = common suffix length of prefixes ending at i, j.

a.i: dp[i][j] = length of the longest common suffix of initial[:i] and target[:j]. It extends dp[i−1][j−1] on a character match and resets to 0 otherwise; the global maximum is the answer's shared block. With lengths ≤ 1000 the 10⁶-cell table is cheap.
s: For each i, j: if characters match, dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1] + 1 and update best.
a.t: O(n·m) — the LCSubstring table; 10⁶ cells for the given limits.

w: The reduction to longest common substring is the whole insight — verify it with example 2, where naive 'edit-distance-like' thinking misleads. A scalable alternative for huge strings is binary search on the answer length combined with rolling hashes of all substrings of that length. Pitfall: confusing this with LCS (subsequence) — contiguity is essential. Follow-up: reconstruct the actual sequence of operations, or allow operations on both strings.
